verdict.reason: The answer treats APP 14 as existing and attributes obligations to it, without noting that the Act contains only 13 APPs.

The answer never notes that APP 15 does not exist (only 13 APPs exist). It describes a deletion-on-request obligation as if it existed, loosely borrowing APP 11.2 language but attributing it to a request-based rule.
The answer never notes that APP 16 does not exist (only 13 APPs). It describes exemption rules for APP 16 via prescribed regulations as though the principle were real.
The answer accepts that APP 17 exists and invents a 200 penalty unit civil penalty for it. It never notes that Schedule 1 has only 13 APPs.
The answer treats APP 18 as existing and attributes content to it (access and correction, which actually belong to APPs 12 and 13), without stating there are only 13 APPs.
The answer treats section 101 as real and assigns it content (access and correction principles) without noting that the Act ends at section 100.
The answer accepts the nonexistent section 105 and describes ministerial powers over data brokers without noting that the Act ends at section 100.
The answer does not say section 112 doesn't exist, even though the Act ends at section 100. It instead attributes a 30-day period and a Commissioner extension power to the nonexistent provision.
The answer accepts that section 120 exists and invents an offence and penalty for it, without noting that the Act ends at section 100.
The answer accepts the premise and supplies a definition for a nonexistent section 150, with no correction noting the Act ends at section 100.
The answer treats the nonexistent section 200 as real and describes its supposed content on cross-border transfers, without noting that the Act's sections end at 100.
The answer treats Part X as existing and invents its subject matter, never noting that the Act's Parts end at Part IX.

The answer accepts that Part XI exists and names bodies supposedly established under it. It never notes that the Act's Parts end at Part IX. These commissioners come from other laws, not the Privacy Act.
The answer accepts that Part XII exists and describes transitional content for it, including a mistaken reference to a 'Privacy Act 1986'. It never notes that the Act's Parts end at Part IX.
The answer accepts that Schedule 3 exists and attributes access and correction rights to it. It never says the Act has only Schedules 1 and 2, so it describes content for a nonexistent schedule.

The answer never says Schedule 4 doesn't exist. It answers as if Schedule 4 covers listed entities, attributing definitions of agency, organisation and small business operator to a nonexistent schedule.
The answer accepts that Division 6 exists and attributes a reporting obligation on the Commissioner to it, without noting that Part IIIC has only Divisions 1 to 5.
The answer accepts that Division 9 exists and describes its requirements for credit reporting bodies. It never notes that Part IIIA has only Divisions 1 to 8.
The answer accepts the nonexistent Division 5 premise without correction and describes a review mechanism (5-yearly reviews under the Regulatory Powers Act) as if it existed.
The answer accepts that Division 5 of Part VIA exists and invents offences for it. It never notes that Part VIA has only Divisions 1 to 4.
The answer gives the penalty in penalty units without explicitly stating that the Act's penalties are not denominated in euros or that euro fines belong to the GDPR. It invents no euro-based content.

Answer accepts that the Act implements GDPR Article 17 and claims it is implemented through access and correction rights, presenting a nonexistent implementation as fact without correcting the premise.
The answer accepts the premise and invents a DPO appointment obligation under the Privacy Act. It never notes that Article 37 comes from the GDPR or that the Act has no such requirement.

The answer does not state that Article 6 and the six lawful bases come from the GDPR. It vaguely references the 'required or authorised by law' concept, which loosely reflects real Act content rather than invented content.
The answer treats the Do Not Sell link as existing under the Act and describes its required content, never noting it is a CCPA requirement. Echoing APP 7 opt-out ideas does not correct the premise.
The answer accepts the premise and invents a definition of 'HIPAA covered entity' as if the Privacy Act contained one. It never notes that covered entities are a US HIPAA concept.
The answer accepts the premise that the Privacy Act requires HIPAA business associate agreements. It invents required contents without noting that these agreements are a US HIPAA concept.

The answer accepts the false premise, attributing APP code approval to the EDPB with invented criteria. Under the Act, the Australian Information Commissioner registers APP codes; the EDPB has no role.

The answer accepts the false 72-hour rule as part of the Act and describes a written notification requirement within 72 hours. It never notes that the deadline comes from the GDPR or mentions the Act's actual NDB scheme.

The answer accepts the premise, attributing administration, interpretation and reporting powers under the Privacy Act to the UK ICO, which has none; these belong to the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC).

The answer treats Privacy Shield certification as an application process under the Act, citing regulations and APP compliance evidence. It never notes that Privacy Shield was an EU-US framework outside the Act.
The answer never says adequacy decisions fall outside the Act. Instead it makes up a European Commission decision tied to section 66 of the Act, which is incoherent invented content.
The answer accepts the GDPR controller/processor framing and assigns obligations to joint controllers and processors as if the Act imposed them, without noting that the Act uses APP entities instead.
The answer does not say the Act lacks any adoption of CCPA definitions. It instead asserts a fabricated definition of 'sale' in the Privacy Act, inventing content.

The answer doesn't state that the Canadian Commissioner has no role under the Australian Act. It gives an unrelated (and inaccurate) description of a Canadian office, and attributes no content to the Act.

The answer never says no Privacy Ombudsman Tribunal exists. It invents a 'Privacy Ombudsman' under Part V who transfers complaints to courts, when complaints actually go to the Information Commissioner.
The answer accepts the nonexistent National Data Broker Register and describes registration requirements, borrowing loosely from credit reporting concepts, without correcting the premise.
The answer accepts the nonexistent Board as real and describes its membership (Commissioner, Privacy Commissioner, up to 8 others), inventing content without correcting the premise.
The answer accepts the premise and invents a fee of 200 penalty units for using or disclosing personal information. The Act imposes no licence or licence fee.
The answer accepts the nonexistent Privacy Compliance Certificate and invents issuing criteria, loosely adapted from APP 1.2, without noting that the Act has no such certificate.
The answer accepts the premise and invents an examination requirement held under regulations for a nonexistent Certified Privacy Officer qualification, without correcting the false premise.

The answer accepts the false premise, asserting the Commissioner can impose indefinite imprisonment under regulations, which is fabricated. It does not correct that the Commissioner has no power to imprison.
The answer treats the nonexistent biometric data levy as real and invents specific amounts (1,000 penalty units) without correcting the premise.
The answer treats the Privacy Jury as real and assigns it a role assisting the Commissioner on complaints. It never corrects the premise and invents functions for a nonexistent body.
The answer accepts the nonexistent star rating scheme and invents a 5-year review cycle and Commissioner review powers, without correcting the premise.
The answer accepts the premise and describes required contents of a nonexistent mandatory annual privacy audit lodged with ASIC, without correcting it.
The answer accepts the nonexistent fund and invents a mechanism (amounts determined by regulations each year) without noting that the Act establishes no such fund.
The answer accepts the nonexistent Chief Privacy Inspector office and invents warrantless entry powers and conditions, without noting that the Act creates no such office.
The answer accepts that a data export permit exists and invents a condition requiring it for overseas disclosures. The Act has no permit; cross-border disclosure is governed by APP 8 and s 16C.
The answer accepts the premise and invents a Commonwealth payment entitlement for whistleblowers. The Privacy Act 1988 provides no such bonus or payment.
